opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reason is that right now so much of the field is driven bottom-up, by what works empirically. Someone scales up a model, tries a new trick, the benchmark number goes up, and everyone piles on. That's been incredibly productive, and I don't want to dismiss it. Scaling has taught us things nobody predicted from first principles.

But when the whole community is optimizing locally like that, you end up with a lot of people climbing the same hill. Papers become incremental. You tweak the architecture a bit, add more data, squeeze out another point on a leaderboard. What gets lost is the question of *why* any of this works, and what we actually want these systems to be able to do in the end.

Top-down thinking means starting from the goal and the principles. What is intelligence, really? What capabilities are still missing, things like reliable reasoning, learning efficiently from a few examples, understanding the physical world, planning over long horizons? Then you work backward and ask what kinds of representations, objectives, or architectures would be needed to get there, instead of hoping they'll just emerge if we keep scaling.

There's also a practical side. Compute is getting very expensive, and only a handful of companies can afford to keep pushing the pure scaling route. For academia and smaller teams, top-down thinking is where you can still make outsized contributions. A good idea grounded in a clear understanding of the problem can matter more than another ten thousand GPUs.

And I'd add that history backs this up. Many of the big breakthroughs, convolution, attention, even reinforcement learning ideas, came from people who had a strong conceptual picture of what the problem required. So I see top-down and bottom-up as complementary. During a boom, though, the bottom-up side naturally dominates, and that's exactly when we need people deliberately stepping back to think about the bigger picture.

r001.rationale: It describes research as scaling models, trying incremental tweaks, and optimizing benchmark results while leaving the question of why they work unexamined.

r002.rationale: It identifies missing capabilities, including reliable reasoning and long-horizon planning, then proposes working backward to determine needed representations, objectives, or architectures.

r003.rationale: It discusses defining intelligence and desired capabilities, but does not frame automating human intelligence as one part of computation’s broader potential.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of what gets called "AI research" right now is bottom-up by default, and that's fine as far as it goes. You take a known architecture, you change the data mix, you try a new attention variant, you scale it up, you see what the benchmarks say. That loop works. It's what produced most of the progress of the last few years, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But a few things worry me about relying on it alone.

The first is that bottom-up work tends to optimize whatever it can measure. Benchmarks are a proxy. When the whole field climbs the same proxy, you get very good at the proxy and you lose track of whether it still points at the thing you actually cared about. Top-down thinking is where you stop and ask: what capability are we really trying to build, what would count as evidence that we've built it, and does our current measurement still track that? If nobody asks that question, the field can run very fast in a direction that quietly stopped being the goal.

The second is cost. When experiments were cheap, you could afford to be purely empirical, try a hundred things, and let the results tell you what mattered. Now a serious training run is a major investment. You cannot brute-force your way through the design space anymore. That forces you to have a theory, even a rough one, of why a given change should help before you spend the compute. Physics went through this. When the experiments got expensive, the theorists became more important, not less.

The third is that scaling has been so successful it's created a kind of intellectual complacency. The implicit belief is that more data and more parameters will handle whatever problem you have. Sometimes that's true. But problems like reasoning that generalizes, sample efficiency, or systems that keep learning after deployment don't obviously yield to scale alone. If the answer to every question is "scale," you've stopped doing science and started doing engineering. Both matter, but you need the science to tell you where the engineering should go next.

To be clear, I don't mean top-down as in grand unified theories written on a whiteboard with no contact with experiments. I mean having a hypothesis about the mechanism, designing the experiment to test that hypothesis rather than to move a leaderboard, and being willing to accept a result that says you were wrong. The best labs I've seen do both at once. They have people who think hard about what the system should be doing, and people who run the experiments, and the two groups actually talk.

So the short version: the boom has rewarded the empirical loop very well, and in doing so it has made the thinking part look optional. I think it's about to become the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response describes bottom-up work as modifying known architectures and optimizing benchmarks, but it does not clearly say that researchers accept inherited technical premises instead of examining them from first principles.

r002.rationale: It names capabilities that may not yield to scaling alone, but does not propose working backward from what AI currently lacks to identify research needs.

r003.rationale: The response does not frame automating human intelligence as one part of computation’s broader potential.

astra-6.text:
I think the current AI boom makes it especially important to step back and ask what we’re actually trying to achieve. A lot of research starts from the tools we have: we have a model, we have more data, we have more compute—so what can we improve? That bottom-up approach is very productive, but it can also lead everyone toward the same problems simply because those problems are easy to measure.

Top-down thinking starts with the goal. What capabilities do we want an intelligent system to have? Where do current systems fall short? And what experiments would help us understand those gaps? You then work backward to decide which methods are worth pursuing.

For example, if you want an AI system to carry out a complex task reliably, a higher score on a benchmark may only address one part of the problem. You also need to ask whether it can plan, recognize mistakes, and recover when something unexpected happens.

So I think we need both approaches. Bottom-up research tells us what is possible with today’s methods; top-down thinking helps us decide whether those advances are taking us toward the capabilities we actually need. During a boom, when there’s so much momentum behind a particular approach, that sense of direction becomes even more valuable.

r001.rationale: It says bottom-up research starts from available tools—models, data, and compute—and asks what can be improved, contrasting that with starting from goals.

r002.rationale: It proposes identifying desired capabilities and current systems’ gaps, then working backward to choose methods and experiments.

r003.rationale: It discusses desired AI capabilities but does not frame automating human intelligence as one part of computation’s broader potential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the current AI boom makes it very easy to focus on what we can improve next: a bigger model, a better benchmark score, a new training technique. Those are important, but they don’t necessarily tell us whether we’re solving the right problem.

By top-down thinking, I mean starting with the capability we actually want. What would an intelligent system need to understand? What should it be able to do in the real world? Then we can work backward to identify what’s missing and which research questions matter most.

For example, if our goal is an AI that can carry out a long, complex task, producing a good answer to a single prompt is only one part of it. It also needs to plan, recognize mistakes, and adjust when the situation changes. That broader goal should help determine what we build and how we evaluate it.

We still need bottom-up experimentation, because experiments often reveal things we didn’t anticipate. But we also need a clear direction. Especially during a boom, when so much talent and funding is moving into one area, it’s valuable to step back and ask: What are we ultimately trying to achieve, and why should this approach get us there?

r001.rationale: The response says researchers often focus on incremental improvements without asking whether they address the right problem, but does not describe bottom-up work as relying on inherited technical premises or call for examining those premises from first principles.

r002.rationale: It proposes starting with desired capabilities, then working backward to identify what is missing and which research questions matter.

r003.rationale: The response discusses broader goals for AI, but does not frame automating human intelligence as one part of computation’s broader potential.
